theory.heading: A system of related views
theory.body: Third-angle projection is a drawing system that represents an object through related two-dimensional views. Each view shows one face or direction while remaining connected to the others. The views are positioned in a recognised arrangement so the reader can compare them and understand the object more clearly. A single view may not show every feature, so information from several views must be combined. Third-angle projection communicates shape and position without relying on a three-dimensional picture.

theory.heading: Front, plan and side views
theory.body: The front view shows the object as seen directly from its selected front. The plan, also called the top view, shows it from directly above. A side view shows the object from an identified side. Each view communicates different visible edges and features. A feature may appear as a shape in one view and as an edge or line in another. These differences do not mean the object has changed. They show the same object from different directions.

theory.heading: Compare position and alignment
theory.body: Related views should be compared by looking for matching positions and aligned features. A feature near one side in the front view should connect logically with its position in the plan and side views. Alignment helps the reader decide which lines represent the same part of the object. Do not invent a feature because one view seems unclear. Return to the related views and written information, then ask about any remaining uncertainty. The unchanged original two-page Footstool drawing remains the sole dimensional and construction authority. Current school SOPs and teacher directions control all actual workshop activity.

questions.question: What is third-angle projection?
choices: A system of related two-dimensional views
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Third-angle projection uses connected two-dimensional views to communicate an object.
questions.retryFeedback: Review A system of related views and focus on the opening definition.

questions.question: Why are several views often needed?
choices: Each view shows a different object
One view may not show every feature
The drawing must fill the page
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Several views combine information that may not be visible from one direction alone.
questions.retryFeedback: Return to A system of related views and identify why a single view may be incomplete.

questions.question: What does third-angle projection communicate without requiring a three-dimensional picture?
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. The related views communicate the shape and position of features.
questions.retryFeedback: Re-read A system of related views and focus on what the drawing system communicates.

questions.question: What does the front view represent?
choices: The object seen from directly above
The object seen from its selected front
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. The front view shows the object from the direction selected as its front.
questions.retryFeedback: Review Front, plan and side views and locate the definition of the front view.

questions.question: Which view shows an object from directly above?
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. The plan, or top view, represents the object from directly above.
questions.retryFeedback: Return to Front, plan and side views and identify the view also called the top view.

questions.question: Why might the same feature look different in two views?
choices: It is represented from different directions
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Viewing direction changes how the same feature appears on the page.
questions.retryFeedback: Re-read Front, plan and side views and focus on how one feature may be shown differently.

questions.question: What is the purpose of comparing aligned features across views?
choices: To identify lines representing the same part
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Alignment helps connect representations of the same feature across related views.
questions.retryFeedback: Review Compare position and alignment and identify what alignment helps the reader decide.

questions.question: A feature appears near one side in the front view. What should the reader do next?
choices: Compare its position in the plan and side views
Assume it is absent from other views
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Comparing related positions helps confirm how the feature is represented across views.
questions.retryFeedback: Return to Compare position and alignment and focus on how positions should connect logically.

questions.question: What should a student do when one view seems unclear?
choices: Return to related views and written information
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Related views and written information should be checked before reaching a conclusion.
questions.retryFeedback: Re-read Compare position and alignment and identify the response to unclear information.

questions.question: What should happen if uncertainty remains after comparing the views?
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Asking prevents unsupported assumptions about the drawing.
questions.retryFeedback: Review the final sentences of Compare position and alignment and identify the response to remaining uncertainty.

written.prompt: Explain how the front, plan and side views work together in third-angle projection to communicate one object.
written.sentenceStarter: The front view shows ___, the plan view shows ___, and the side view shows ___. Together, they help the reader ___.
written.example: The front view shows the object from its selected front, the plan view shows it from above, and the side view shows it from one side. Together, they help the reader compare aligned features and understand the object's shape and position.
